facts.statement: The study used a mouse model of asphyxial cardiac arrest followed by cardiopulmonary resuscitation.
facts.subject: animals

facts.statement: Researchers measured blood-brain barrier leakage over a period from 3 hours to 14 days after resuscitation.
facts.subject: animals

facts.statement: Scientists collected and analyzed serum exosomes from the mice at one day and three days after the procedure.
facts.subject: animals

facts.statement: The team injected exosomes directly into the brains of other mice to test how they affected brain barrier integrity and microglial cell markers.
facts.subject: animals

facts.statement: In separate lab dishes, brain immune cells taken from the injured mice were treated with exosomes to measure changes in inflammatory markers.
facts.subject: cells_or_tissue

facts.statement: The resuscitation procedure caused temporary damage to the blood-brain barrier that was worst three days later.
facts.subject: animals

facts.statement: Giving exosomes from three days after CPR made brain barrier leakage worse and pushed immune cells toward a harmful inflammatory state more than exosomes from one day after.
facts.subject: animals

facts.statement: The authors conclude that these findings point to exosomes as a possible cause of brain injury after CPR and suggest they are a target for future study.
